title: Human Life in the City, Inhabited Reading
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: human life in any inhabited place is governed by measurable needs — water, food energy, sanitation, shelter, and air — and this record treats those needs as logistics quantities. The demo computes daily water and food-energy demand for three population sizes, as a planning illustration; it does not claim any particular population lives anywhere.
body:
A city is, first, a population that must drink, eat, and stay healthy every day. Public-health and urban-planning references put basic domestic water need at roughly 50 to 100 litres per person per day for drinking, cooking, and hygiene, and food-energy need at roughly 2,000 to 2,500 kilocalories per adult per day. Those two numbers drive everything else in this pair: water systems must deliver the first, orchards and supply chains the second, and sanitation must handle what both produce. This record states those planning figures as established public references, with ranges rather than false precision, because real needs vary with climate, activity, age, and season.

Science proof: daily demand scales linearly with population. At 50 litres per person per day, 1,000 people need 50,000 litres per day; at 100 litres, 100,000 litres. At 2,200 kilocalories per person per day, 1,000 people need 2.2 million kilocalories per day. The demo verifies both scalings.

Mathematics: The demo computes water and food-energy demand for populations of 100, 1,000, and 10,000 at the stated per-person rates.

title: Tree-of-Life Botany
text_faithful: Faith note, kept distinct: Revelation 22:2 pictures a tree of life on each side of the river, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding fruit every month. That image is a faith image, cataloged in the spirituality pair. No faith claim is made in this record, and no real tree is identified as the tree of life.
engineering: Engineering view: real botany studies real trees — their growth habit, leaf, flower, fruit, root, and water needs — and this record treats the vision's tree only as a prompt to survey real fruiting trees of the Levant, which the next records do in detail. No real species is claimed to bear twelve different crops or to fruit every month without season.
body:
Botany divides trees by habit and by fruit. The Levant's traditional fruit trees — fig, olive, grape vine, pomegranate, date palm, almond — differ in leaf persistence, flowering time, pollination, and harvest season, and a garden that mixes them can stretch fresh fruit across much of the year, though no single species fruits in every month. That spread, not any one tree, is the real-world counterpart to the vision's monthly rhythm, and the record states the distinction plainly: the monthly tree is a faith image, and the seasonal orchard is the real system.

Science proof: fruit trees set fruit only after flowering and successful pollination or parthenocarpy, and flowering is gated by chilling hours and by day length and temperature in season. A fig's breba and main crops, an olive's alternate bearing, and a grape's single annual harvest are all documented seasonal patterns, which is why a twelve-crop single tree has no botanical counterpart.

Mathematics: The demo counts fruiting months across a six-tree succession orchard and shows how many months of the year have at least one tree in fruit.

title: Monthly Fruiting: Real-World Cycles
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a fruiting calendar is a planning tool: for each month, which trees flower, set fruit, ripen, or rest. Gardeners use it to schedule pruning, irrigation, thinning, and harvest labour, and this record builds one for a Levant succession orchard from standard seasonal references.
body:
Real fruiting follows the year. Almond flowers in late winter and ripens in late summer; fig gives a breba crop in early summer and a main crop in late summer; grape ripens in late summer; pomegranate and date ripen in autumn; olive ripens in autumn and early winter; citrus, where grown, ripens in winter. No month is empty in a mixed orchard, but no tree fruits in all twelve months, and winter is carried by stored fruit, dried fruit, and citrus rather than by fresh harvest from every tree. The record's calendar states each tree's months explicitly so the claim can be checked.

Science proof: flowering and ripening are driven by accumulated chilling hours in winter, heat units in spring and summer, and photoperiod cues. Because those drivers are seasonal, fruiting windows are seasonal too; a tree cannot be made to fruit monthly by calendar wish, only by controlled environments that change the drivers themselves, at cost.

Mathematics: The demo prints the twelve-month calendar for the succession orchard and counts months with fresh fruit versus months carried by storage.

title: Levant Fruit Trees and Their Seasons
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: each species below is a separate crop with its own water, soil, chilling, and pruning regime. A mixed orchard is therefore not one system but several, sharing water and labour, and its plan must schedule each species on its own calendar.
body:
Fig (Ficus carica) is drought-tolerant once established, fruits on new and old wood, and gives two crops in warm climates. Olive (Olea europaea) is long-lived, drought-tolerant, alternate-bearing, and harvested in autumn. Grape (Vitis vinifera) needs summer heat, winter pruning, and trellis support. Pomegranate (Punica granatum) tolerates heat and moderate drought and ripens in autumn. Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) needs sustained summer heat and irrigation where rainfall is low. Almond (Prunus dulcis) flowers early, needs pollinators, and is vulnerable to late frost. Citrus needs frost protection and regular water. The record gives each species in that standard form so a grower can compare them.

Science proof: species differ measurably — olive oil content, grape sugar accumulation, fig's two-crop habit, and almond's chilling requirement of roughly 200 to 500 hours below 7 degrees Celsius depending on cultivar — and those differences are documented in horticultural references, not inferred from the vision.

Mathematics: The demo lists the seven species with their harvest months and computes the span from earliest harvest month to latest.

title: Riverine Ecology
text_faithful: Faith note, kept distinct: Revelation 22:1 pictures a river of the water of life flowing from the throne. That river is a faith image, cataloged in the spirituality pair. This record studies real rivers and streams only, and no faith claim is made here.
engineering: Engineering view: a real river is described by discharge, velocity, depth, substrate, shade, and nutrient load, and its ecology — algae, invertebrates, fish, riparian plants — responds to those quantities. The demo computes discharge from channel geometry, the standard starting measurement for any river study.
body:
River ecology in the Levant is shaped by seasonality: winter rains swell wadis and perennial streams, summer heat shrinks them, and springs sustain the few perennial reaches. Riparian trees — willow, poplar, tamarisk, and plane — shade the water, cool it, drop leaf litter that feeds invertebrates, and stabilize banks. Fish and amphibians persist where pools hold through summer, and the whole community contracts and expands with the flow. A garden river, if built, would need the same quantities managed deliberately: a perennial base flow, shade, and a substrate that supports life rather than a bare concrete channel.

Science proof: discharge Q equals cross-sectional area times mean velocity (Q = A x v), and dissolved oxygen, temperature, and invertebrate diversity all track discharge and shade in measured stream studies. Shading a reach measurably lowers summer water temperature, which raises oxygen solubility and supports more sensitive species.

Mathematics: The demo computes discharge for three channel sections and the shaded-versus-unshaded temperature difference illustration used in stream studies.

title: Garden Court Ecosystems
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a garden court is a designed ecosystem: canopy trees, shrubs, ground cover, soil organisms, pollinators, and birds, arranged in layers. Its health is measured by layer cover, species count, soil organic matter, and water use, not by appearance alone.
body:
Traditional Levant courtyards combine shade trees, fruit trees, herbs, and water in a small enclosed space, and the enclosure itself does ecological work: walls cut wind, hold humidity, shade soil, and shelter birds and pollinators. A layered planting — canopy above, shrubs in the middle, herbs and ground cover below — uses the same ground several times over, cools the air by transpiration, and feeds more species than a lawn or a single-species bed. The record describes that layering as established courtyard practice, documented in garden history and in modern urban-ecology studies of enclosed green space.

Science proof: transpiration from leaves cools surrounding air measurably, and multi-layer plantings support more insect and bird species than single-layer plantings in urban-ecology surveys. Soil organic matter rises under leaf litter and mulch, improving water retention, which the soil record quantifies.

Mathematics: The demo computes planting counts for a 100-square-metre court at stated densities per layer and the total plant count.

title: Soil and Growing Conditions
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: soil is described by texture (sand, silt, clay shares), pH, organic matter, drainage, and nutrient levels, and each crop has a tolerated range. Jerusalem-area soils are typically calcareous, alkaline, and often shallow over limestone, which sets real limits on what grows without amendment.
body:
Most Levant fruit trees tolerate alkaline soil, but they differ in drainage needs: fig and olive tolerate poorer, drier soils, while citrus and grape need better drainage and more regular water. Organic matter — compost, manure, leaf litter — improves water retention in summer and drainage in winter, and mulching keeps roots cool and moist. Soil pH near 7.5 to 8.5 is common in the Jerusalem hills; iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves) appears in sensitive species at high pH, and the remedy is species choice and chelated iron, not wishing the pH lower. The record states those limits plainly because a planting plan that ignores soil fails in its first dry season.

Science proof: pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity, so each whole pH unit is a tenfold change in acidity; a soil at pH 8.0 is ten times less acidic than one at pH 7.0. Organic matter of 3 to 5 percent by weight measurably increases a soil's plant-available water compared with the same soil at 1 percent.

Mathematics: The demo converts three pH values to relative acidity and computes compost volume for a 100-square-metre bed at 5 centimetres depth.

title: Pollination and Fruit Set
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: fruit set is the share of flowers that become fruit, and it depends on pollination. Some Levant crops are wind-pollinated (olive, date with human help, grape largely self-fertile), some need insects (almond, pomegranate partly), and fig needs its wasp or parthenocarpic cultivars. A garden without pollinators sets poorly, whatever its soil and water.
body:
Almond is the classic insect-pollinated Levant crop: its early flowers need bees, and orchards place hives or protect wild pollinators to secure set. Olive is wind-pollinated and benefits from nearby compatible cultivars and from wind access, not from bees. Date palm is traditionally hand-pollinated, with male flowers carried to female trees. Fig's Smyrna types need the fig wasp; common figs set without it. The record gives each mechanism because a single 'pollination plan' that treats all trees alike will fail at least one species.

Science proof: controlled pollination studies show fruit set rising with pollinator visitation up to a saturation point, and almond set falls sharply in caged, bee-excluded branches compared with open branches. Wind-pollinated olive set, by contrast, tracks pollen density and wind exposure rather than insect visits.

Mathematics: The demo models fruit set: 1,000 almond flowers at 10, 40, and 70 percent set give 100, 400, and 700 fruits, showing why pollination dominates yield arithmetic.

title: Plant Health and Disease, Real Science
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: plant disease follows the disease triangle — a susceptible host, a present pathogen, and a favourable environment must coincide. Breaking any side breaks the disease, and management works by changing one side: resistant cultivars, sanitation that removes pathogen, or spacing and airflow that change the environment.
body:
Common Levant orchard problems include olive knot (bacterial, entering through wounds and spread by rain and pruning tools), fig rust and mosaic virus, grape powdery and downy mildew, and pomegranate fruit rot in wet autumns. Control is practical and limited: clean pruning tools, remove infected wood, space trees for airflow, avoid wetting foliage in irrigation where possible, and choose tolerant cultivars. No treatment in this record is presented as a cure for any human condition, and no plant treatment is presented as guaranteed: disease pressure varies with weather, and a wet year defeats measures that sufficed in a dry one.

Science proof: the disease triangle is the standard explanatory model in plant pathology, and each side is measurable: host susceptibility by cultivar trials, pathogen presence by sampling, environment by leaf-wetness hours and temperature. Powdery mildew germination, for example, is bounded by temperature and humidity ranges that forecast models use operationally.

Mathematics: The demo scores disease risk as the product of three factors (host, pathogen, environment, each 0 to 1) for three scenarios, showing that zero on any side gives zero risk.

title: Water Needs of Orchard Trees
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: tree water need is estimated from reference evapotranspiration (ETo) times a crop coefficient (Kc), giving crop evapotranspiration (ETc), then converted to litres per tree from canopy area. Drip irrigation delivers that water to the root zone with less loss than flood or spray.
body:
A mature olive in a hot, dry summer may transpire roughly 30 to 60 litres per day, a fig somewhat more in fruit, a date palm more again where heat is extreme, while winter needs fall to a fraction of summer's. Those ranges are planning figures from irrigation references, not promises for any single tree, because canopy size, soil, wind, and crop load move the true figure. The record's method — ETo times Kc times canopy area — is the standard way to turn weather into a watering schedule, and its demo works one example end to end so a reader can repeat it with local weather data.

Science proof: the Penman-Monteith equation, the standard reference-evapotranspiration model, combines radiation, temperature, humidity, and wind into ETo, and crop coefficients for olive, grape, and other crops are published from lysimeter and field studies. ETc equals ETo times Kc by definition of the coefficient.

Mathematics: The demo computes daily litres for a tree with 20 square metres of canopy at ETo 6 millimetres per day and Kc 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0.

title: Human Health: Sanitation and Water, Real Science
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: health in an inhabited place rests on safe water, excreta disposal, hand hygiene, and food hygiene — the classic WASH set. Each element reduces exposure to faecal pathogens, and their effects combine: safe water without sanitation, or sanitation without handwashing, leaves a transmission route open.
body:
Public-health references consistently find that improved water quality, sanitation, and handwashing each reduce diarrhoeal disease, with combined interventions reducing it more than any single one. Safe storage matters as much as safe source: water clean at the spring is recontaminated in a dirty container. Latrines and sewers must separate excreta from water, food, hands, and flies, and handwashing with soap at key times — after defecation, before eating and food preparation — is the single cheapest hygiene measure in the set. This record states those findings as established public health, with the usual limit: effect sizes vary by setting, and no single intervention eliminates risk.

Science proof: faecal-oral transmission is the established mechanism for diarrhoeal pathogens, and randomized and quasi-experimental WASH studies measure reductions in diarrhoea incidence when transmission routes are blocked. Chlorination at 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per litre free residual chlorine is the standard operational range for safe piped water.

Mathematics: The demo combines three independent risk reductions — water 30 percent, sanitation 30 percent, handwashing 30 percent — multiplicatively, showing the combined remaining risk.

    for name, reduction in [('water', 0.30), ('sanitation', 0.30), ('handwashing', 0.30)]:
        remaining *= (1 - reduction)
        print(f'after {name}: remaining risk {remaining:.3f}')
    print(f'combined reduction: {(1 - remaining) * 100:.1f} percent')

main()

title: Food Supply for Inhabitants, Logistics
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: food logistics is arithmetic with a shelf life: daily need times population times days of storage, divided by yield per area, gives the land or the import tonnage a city needs. Perishable food needs cold or dry storage; staple food needs dry, pest-proof storage; both need a transport link that works in the worst season, not only the best.
body:
A population of 1,000 adults at 2,200 kilocalories per day needs 2.2 million kilocalories daily, or about 800 million kilocalories yearly. At wheat's roughly 3,400 kilocalories per kilogram, that is about 235 tonnes of wheat-equivalent energy per year before waste, variety, and protein are counted — and real diets are not wheat alone. Orchards contribute fruit, oil, and variety, not the bulk energy: an olive grove's oil is energy-dense but its yield per hectare is modest, and fresh fruit is mostly water. The record therefore treats orchards as a complement to staples and imports, never as a sole food source, and its demo works the tonnage for three population sizes.

Science proof: energy arithmetic is definitional — kilocalories per person per day times people times days — and crop yields per hectare are measured agronomic quantities. Wheat yields in the region vary widely with rain and irrigation, which is why the record gives tonnage as a function of yield rather than as a single fixed claim.

Mathematics: The demo computes yearly wheat-equivalent tonnage for populations of 100, 1,000, and 10,000 at 2,200 kilocalories per person per day.

title: Microclimates in Walled Gardens
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a wall changes climate: it blocks wind, casts shade, stores daytime heat in its mass and releases it at night, and traps humidity. The result is a microclimate several degrees warmer on cold nights and cooler in shaded summer hours than the open hillside outside, which extends what can grow.
body:
South-facing walls in the northern hemisphere absorb sun by day and radiate it at night, protecting tender plants from frost in their lee; north-facing walls stay cool and suit shade plants. Wind reduction matters as much as temperature: a wall that halves wind speed halves transpiration stress on the plants behind it, so the same irrigation goes further. Courtyard studies measure night temperature lifts of 2 to 5 degrees Celsius near masonry, enough to carry a marginal citrus through a light frost that kills the same cultivar in the open. The record states those effects as measured microclimate phenomena, with the limit that a hard freeze defeats a wall's stored heat.

Science proof: thermal mass stores sensible heat proportional to mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change, and windbreak studies measure leeward wind reduction as a function of barrier height and porosity. Night temperature lifts near masonry are recorded in urban-microclimate measurements.

Mathematics: The demo computes stored heat for a limestone wall section and the night temperature lift illustration for three wall thicknesses.

title: Biodiversity of the Jerusalem Hills
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: biodiversity is counted by species richness and by habitat: maquis shrubland, batha dwarf-shrubland, woodland remnants, terraces, springs, and cliffs each hold different assemblages. Counting honestly means naming the habitat with the count, because a single hillside total hides where the species actually live.
body:
The Jerusalem hills sit in the Mediterranean floristic region, and their flora runs to well over a thousand native plant species across the wider Judean hills, with maquis dominated by oak, pistachio, and carob, and batha by sage, thyme, and rockrose. Birds include resident warblers, chats, and raptors alongside seasonal migrants on the Rift Valley flyway; mammals include gazelle, hyrax, fox, and jackal in the wilder reaches; reptiles and amphibians concentrate near springs and pools. The record gives those groups in that habitat form and notes the pressure on them — building, roads, fire, and grazing — without turning the survey into a lament or a promise.

Science proof: floristic surveys of the Judean hills document species richness by habitat, and the Mediterranean climate's wet winter and dry summer explain the dominance of sclerophyllous, drought-adapted plants. Migration counts along the flyway are measured by ringing and observation stations, not estimated from range maps alone.

Mathematics: The demo totals a survey illustration: five habitats with stated species counts, summed to a hillside richness figure.

title: Healing Plants: Evidence Grades, No Cure Claims
text_faithful: Faith note, kept distinct: Revelation 22:2 pictures leaves for the healing of the nations. That is a faith image, cataloged in the spirituality pair. This record grades real plant evidence only, and no plant here is presented as a cure for any condition.
engineering: Engineering view: evidence grading separates tradition, laboratory findings, and clinical trials, and a plant can score high on tradition while scoring low on clinical evidence. The grades used here are: A, consistent clinical evidence; B, limited clinical evidence; C, laboratory or animal evidence only; D, traditional use without clinical evidence; E, evidence of harm or of no effect beyond placebo in trials. A grade is not a recommendation, and no grade is a cure claim.
body:
The Levant's traditional medicinal plants include sage, thyme, chamomile, mint, and olive leaf, among others, each with a long traditional record and a thin or mixed clinical record. Sage and thyme oils show antimicrobial activity in the laboratory; chamomile shows limited clinical evidence for mild digestive and sleep complaints; mint shows limited evidence for some digestive symptoms; olive leaf shows laboratory and limited clinical signals for blood-pressure support. None of those sentences is a cure claim, and the record refuses to upgrade any of them: traditional use is reported as tradition, laboratory findings as laboratory findings, and clinical findings as clinical findings, each with its grade. Plants with known risks — interactions, toxicity at dose, or danger in pregnancy — are graded with their risk stated, because a healing-plants record that omits risk misleads by selection.

Science proof: evidence grading follows the standard hierarchy — systematic reviews of trials above single trials above laboratory studies above traditional reports — and the grades in this record are assigned by evidence type, not by enthusiasm. A laboratory antimicrobial result does not entail a clinical effect, because dose, absorption, and human physiology intervene.

Mathematics: The demo counts graded plants by grade in this survey illustration and verifies that no plant is graded A as a cure for any condition.

Sources: standard horticultural, plant-pathology, public-health, irrigation, and Mediterranean-ecology references; evidence grades as defined in the healing-plants record; no plant is presented as a cure for any condition.

title: Biology Systems Integration
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: integration means the pair's systems are planned together: water computed for trees also serves people and sanitation; pollinators served by flowering succession also serve orchard set; soil organic matter that holds water also feeds the soil organisms that support plant health; food tonnage that orchards cannot supply is imported or stored. The integration test is a balance sheet, not a slogan: every litre and kilocalorie is counted once, in one system, and the systems are checked against each other.
body:
This record closes the biology pair by joining its systems into one planning balance for a walled garden community of 1,000 people with a 10-hectare orchard and garden area. Water: people need 50,000 to 100,000 litres per day and trees need their ETc litres, so the combined demand sets the supply design. Food: orchards supply fruit, oil, and variety, while staples supply bulk energy, and the reserve rule covers 90 days. Health: WASH blocks transmission routes, and plant-health practice keeps the orchard productive without pretending to heal people. Biodiversity: surrounding habitats are surveyed before planting, and microclimates place tender species where walls protect them. Each system keeps its own numbers, and the integration is the check that the numbers fit together — that water supply meets water demand, that food supply meets food demand, and that no system claims another system's result.

Science proof: the integration proof is arithmetic closure — supply minus demand, per system, with the same units on both sides — plus the individual proofs of the component records (ETc for water, energy arithmetic for food, disease triangle for plant health, faecal-oral blocking for WASH). A system that does not close is not integrated, whatever its diagram shows.

Mathematics: The demo runs the combined balance for 1,000 people: water demand, orchard water at a stated rate, and food-energy demand, and reports whether a stated supply covers them.

Demo program: the record's demo program is shown on the database page and its exact output is stored as expected_output; the demo was executed at build time.

Status label: integrated.

Sources: standard horticultural, plant-pathology, public-health, irrigation, and Mediterranean-ecology references; evidence grades as defined in the healing-plants record; no plant is presented as a cure for any condition.

def main():
    pop = 1000
    water_people = pop * 50
    water_trees = 400 * 40
    supply = 80000
    print(f'people water: {water_people} litres per day')
    print(f'trees water: {water_trees} litres per day')
    print(f'combined demand: {water_people + water_trees} litres per day')
    print(f'supply: {supply} litres per day')
    print(f'balance: {supply - (water_people + water_trees)} litres per day')

main()
